title: Signals and Systems
tagline: Continuous- and discrete-time signals, LTI systems, convolution, Fourier, Laplace and z-transforms, and sampling
summary: Signals carry information and systems transform them. This course develops the theory of linear time-invariant systems in continuous and discrete time: convolution, Fourier series and transforms, the Laplace and z-transforms, frequency response, and the sampling theorem that links the analog and digital worlds.
overview: A **signal** is a quantity that varies with time (or space) and carries information: the voltage on a microphone lead, the current in a power line, the samples streaming out of an analog-to-digital converter, the pixels of an image. A **system** is anything that takes a signal in and gives a signal out: an amplifier, a filter, a communication channel, a motor and its controller, a few lines of code in a phone. Signals and systems is the common language of electrical engineering for describing both, independently of whether the system is built from resistors, transistors, gears or software.

The course is built around one idea. If a system is **linear** and **time-invariant** (LTI), its whole behaviour is captured by a single signal, its impulse response, and the output for any input is the convolution of the input with that response. Complex exponentials $e^{st}$ and $z^n$ pass through an LTI system unchanged in shape, merely scaled by the system function, so decomposing signals into exponentials — the Fourier series, the Fourier transform, the Laplace and $z$-transforms — turns convolution into multiplication and differential or difference equations into algebra. That is why filters are specified in the frequency domain, why stability is read from pole locations and why a digital signal processor can imitate an analog filter.

We treat continuous and discrete time side by side: signals and their transformations, system properties, convolution, Fourier series, the continuous-time and discrete-time Fourier transforms, sampling (the bridge between the two worlds), and finally the Laplace and $z$-transforms, which extend Fourier analysis to unstable signals and give the pole–zero picture used throughout control and filter design. The mathematics of the transforms themselves is developed in the Maths Atlas; here the emphasis is on what the transforms mean for engineering systems.

The difficulty is less in any single calculation than in holding several viewpoints at once — time and frequency, continuous and discrete, a signal and its transform — and moving between them fluently. Work every example in both domains when you can, sketch signals before computing with them, and keep track of units ($\mathrm{rad/s}$ versus $\mathrm{Hz}$, radians per sample versus cycles per sample): most mistakes in this subject are mistakes of bookkeeping rather than of understanding.
outcomes: Classify signals as continuous or discrete, periodic or aperiodic, energy or power, and transform them by shifting, scaling and reversing the independent variable.
Determine whether a system is linear, time-invariant, causal, stable, memoryless and invertible, and justify the answer from its input–output description.
Compute the output of an LTI system by convolution in continuous and discrete time, and relate the impulse response to differential and difference equation models.
Expand periodic signals in Fourier series and predict the steady-state response of an LTI system to a periodic input.
Use the continuous-time and discrete-time Fourier transforms and their properties to analyse filtering, modulation and frequency response.
State and derive the sampling theorem, predict aliasing, and design anti-aliasing and reconstruction filters for a sampled-data system.
Apply the Laplace and $z$-transforms with their regions of convergence to find system functions, impulse responses and stability from poles and zeros.
Move between time-domain, frequency-domain and pole–zero descriptions of the same system and choose the one that makes a given problem simplest.

chapters.title: Signals
chapters.summary: Continuous- and discrete-time signals, transformations of the independent variable, exponentials, sinusoids, steps and impulses, energy and power.

chapters.title: Systems and their properties
chapters.summary: Linearity, time invariance, causality, stability, memory and invertibility, and interconnections of systems.

chapters.title: LTI systems and convolution
chapters.summary: The impulse response, convolution sums and integrals, and differential and difference equation models.

chapters.title: Fourier series
chapters.summary: Fourier series of periodic signals in continuous and discrete time and the response of LTI systems to periodic inputs.

chapters.title: The continuous-time Fourier transform
chapters.summary: The Fourier transform and its properties, frequency response, filtering and the convolution theorem.

chapters.title: The discrete-time Fourier transform
chapters.summary: The DTFT, its properties and the frequency response of discrete-time systems.

chapters.title: Sampling
chapters.summary: The sampling theorem, aliasing, ideal and practical reconstruction, and discrete-time processing of continuous-time signals.

chapters.title: The Laplace transform
chapters.summary: The bilateral and unilateral Laplace transform, regions of convergence, system functions, poles, zeros and stability.

chapters.title: The z-transform
chapters.summary: The z-transform, regions of convergence, inverse transforms, and system functions of difference equations.

history.title: Laplace's generating integrals
history.detail: In the Théorie analytique des probabilités Pierre-Simon Laplace used integrals of the form now called the Laplace transform to solve difference and differential equations in probability.

history.title: Fourier's theory of heat
history.detail: Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur expanded arbitrary functions in trigonometric series to solve the heat equation, the origin of Fourier series and, later, the Fourier integral.

history.title: Heaviside's operational calculus
history.detail: Oliver Heaviside treated the derivative as an algebraic operator to solve transmission-line and circuit equations, introducing the unit step; the Laplace transform later gave his methods a rigorous footing.

history.title: The Gibbs phenomenon
history.detail: Prompted by overshoot seen in Albert Michelson's mechanical harmonic analyser, J. Willard Gibbs explained in letters to Nature that Fourier partial sums of a discontinuous function overshoot by about 9 % of the jump however many terms are taken.

history.title: Nyquist on telegraph transmission
history.detail: Harry Nyquist showed that a channel of bandwidth $W$ can carry at most $2W$ independent pulse values per second, the rate now bearing his name.

history.title: Kotelnikov's sampling theorem
history.detail: Vladimir Kotelnikov proved that a band-limited signal is determined by samples taken at twice its highest frequency, in a paper for the first All-Union conference on communications.

history.title: Shannon's sampling theorem
history.detail: Claude Shannon's paper Communication in the Presence of Noise stated and proved the sampling theorem with the sinc interpolation formula, building on the cardinal series of E. T. Whittaker (1915).

history.title: The z-transform named
history.detail: John Ragazzini and Lotfi Zadeh introduced the name and systematic use of the z-transform for sampled-data control systems at Columbia University.

history.title: The fast Fourier transform
history.detail: James Cooley and John Tukey published an algorithm computing the discrete Fourier transform of $N$ points in about $N\log_2 N$ operations, making spectral analysis practical on digital computers.

references.title: Signals and Systems (2nd ed.)
references.authors: Alan V. Oppenheim, Alan S. Willsky, S. Hamid Nawab
references.note: The standard text, treating continuous and discrete time in parallel; this course follows its notation and order closely.

references.title: Linear Systems and Signals (3rd ed.)
references.note: Very readable, with many worked examples and a careful treatment of the Laplace transform and system response.

references.title: Signals and Systems (2nd ed.)
references.note: Strong on applications to communications and control, with good problem sets.

references.title: Discrete-Time Signal Processing (3rd ed.)
references.authors: Alan V. Oppenheim, Ronald W. Schafer
references.note: The next step after this course: sampling, the z-transform and filter design in depth.

references.title: The Fourier Transform and Its Applications (3rd ed.)
references.note: A classic for intuition about transforms, with pictorial transform pairs and physical examples.

references.title: Signals and Systems: Analysis Using Transform Methods and MATLAB (2nd ed.)
references.note: Detailed derivations and computational examples; useful for checking your own calculations numerically.
